slides.headline: This Webinar Was Built By [ACCENT]The Thing It Is Selling[/ACCENT]
slides.sub: Every slide. The voice reading them. The page you are watching it on. One config file, one command, one server nobody bills me for.
slides.narration: Before I tell you anything about what this is, I want you to notice something about what you are already looking at. This slide. The voice reading it to you. The page this video is sitting inside. None of it was shot in a studio. Nobody edited it. I did not open a video editor one single time. I wrote one file, I ran one command, and this came out the other end. That is the entire pitch, and you are already inside the proof of it. So let me show you how it works.

slides.headline: What it took to make [ACCENT]what you are watching[/ACCENT]
slides.narration: Here are the real numbers behind this video. Thirty nine slides, and not one of them is hand written markup. They are entries in a list. One config file holds all of it, the slides, every word of the narration, and the sales page you are on right now. And the running cost is zero dollars a month, because it renders on a machine I already pay for anyway. No account. No key. No per render fee. Hold on to that last number, because we are coming back to it later and it is the whole argument.

slides.kicker: What You Will Walk Away With
slides.headline: By the end of this you will know [ACCENT]exactly[/ACCENT] how to make one
slides.sub: For your product. In your voice. On your own server.
slides.narration: So here is what I am going to do with the next twenty five minutes. I am going to take the three beliefs that stop most people from ever making a webinar, and I am going to break them one at a time. And for each one I will show you the specific piece of this tool that does the breaking. By the end you will know what a webinar actually costs to produce when you own the machine that makes it. Not as a theory. You are watching the answer play right now.

slides.headline: I built this for [ACCENT]one[/ACCENT] webinar. Then I could not build the second.
slides.sub: The first one worked. That was the problem.
slides.narration: Let me tell you where this came from, because it did not start life as a product. I needed one webinar. So I did what everybody does. I hand wrote the slide deck as a single web page, I wrote a build script for that one specific deck, and I got it finished. It worked. It looked good. I was pleased with myself. And then about two weeks later I needed a second webinar, I sat down to make it, and I realised I could not. Not without doing the whole thing over. Let me show you why.

slides.kicker: Why The Second One Was Impossible
slides.headline: Everything was welded to the [ACCENT]first[/ACCENT] one
bullets: A hand-written HTML deck — 96 kilobytes of markup, per webinar
A build script hardcoded to that deck's slide count and class names
Binary paths pointing at one specific laptop, in one home folder
A capture step that spawned a server on a fixed port and collided with itself
Change one line of narration and the whole thing re-rendered from zero
slides.narration: Here is what I was actually staring at. A ninety six kilobyte page I had typed by hand, for one webinar. A build script that knew that deck's exact slide count and its exact class names, which meant it worked for that deck and absolutely nothing else. File paths pointing at one laptop, in one home folder, on one operating system. And a capture step that started a little web server on a fixed port, so two builds running at once fought each other for it. To make a second webinar I would have had to do every bit of that again.

slides.headline: So I stopped writing decks. I started writing [ACCENT]data[/ACCENT].
slides.sub: A slide is not markup. It is a layout name and a few fields.
slides.narration: And that is the moment it clicked. A slide is not a page of markup. A slide is a shape with your words in it. A headline slide. A bullet slide. A side by side comparison. Those same shapes repeat in every webinar anyone has ever given. So I wrote the shapes one time, and after that a slide was just a layout name, a handful of fields, and what to say over it. Nine layouts covered every slide I had ever built by hand. And the second webinar took an afternoon.

slides.headline: The tool started building its own [ACCENT]sales page[/ACCENT] too
slides.sub: Same file. Same command. The deck, the video, and the page that sells it.
slides.narration: Then I pushed it one step further, because a video on its own does not sell anything. It needs a page around it. So I gave the page exactly the same treatment. Nine section types, listed in whatever order you want them, living in the same file as the slides. Which means the page you are looking at right now came out of the same config that produced this video, in the same run of the same command. The webinar and the funnel around it are one file. That is not a demonstration. That is the thing you are inside of.

slides.headline: One belief is in the way. [ACCENT]Everything else falls with it.[/ACCENT]
slides.narration: Now, I have shown this to enough people to know exactly what happens next. It is never a question about the software. Nobody asks me about the software. It is always a belief, it is almost always the same one, and until that belief moves, nothing else I say is going to land. So let me put it on the screen in the words people actually use when they say it to me.

slides.quote: "Making a webinar is a production. I do not have the setup, I do not have the voice for it, and the tools that would do it for me cost more every month than the thing I am trying to sell."
slides.narration: That is it. Near enough word for word, that is the wall. And I want you to notice something about it. That is not one objection. That is three separate objections stacked on top of each other, wearing a trench coat, pretending to be one. One of them is about the work. One of them is about you. And one of them is about the tools. Every single one of the three is wrong, and I am going to take them down in that order.

slides.headline: If a webinar is [ACCENT]one file and one command[/ACCENT], the rest stops mattering
slides.sub: So that is the one we knock over first.
slides.narration: Because those three are not equal. One of them holds the other two up. If making a webinar genuinely is a week long production, then yes, everything else follows and you probably should not bother. But if it is one file and one command, then the camera question and the monthly bill question both change shape completely. So that is the domino. Knock that one over and the other two fall on their own. Secret number one.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]Vehicle[/ACCENT]
slides.sub: What making a webinar actually costs you in effort.
slides.narration: Secret number one is about the vehicle. Not about you, not about money yet. Just about the work itself. What does it genuinely take, in hours and in equipment, to put a narrated webinar in front of another human being. Here is what almost everybody believes, and here is where almost everybody stops.

slides.lie: "Making a webinar means a studio, a camera, and a week."
slides.truth: The truth: it is [ACCENT]one config file[/ACCENT] and [ACCENT]one command[/ACCENT].
slides.sub: No studio. No camera. Not a week.
slides.narration: Making a webinar means a studio, a camera, and a week. That is the belief, and I understand where it comes from, because for a long time that is exactly what it meant. But it is wrong. It is one config file and one command. You write the slides as data and the narration as text, in the same file, and then you run build. What comes back is a rendered video and a page to put it on. There is no studio anywhere in that sentence. There is no camera in that sentence. And it is not a week.

slides.headline: The whole webinar, in [ACCENT]plain text[/ACCENT]
bullets: A brand block — your product name and your colours
A voice block — which cloned voice reads it, and how steady
A slides list — a layout name, a few fields, and what to say
A landing block — the page sections, in the order they appear
A pronunciation map — so your domain gets spoken, not spelled
slides.narration: So what is actually inside that file. A brand block, which is your product name and your colours. A voice block, saying which cloned voice reads the deck and how steady you want the delivery to be. A slides list, where every slide is a layout name, a few fields, and the words you want spoken over it. A landing block, which is your page sections in the order you want them. And a pronunciation map, so the voice says your domain out loud instead of spelling it at people letter by letter. That is the file. That is all of it.

slides.headline: [ACCENT]build[/ACCENT] — and then you have a funnel
slides.sub: Deck, narration, capture, video, landing page. One pass, and every stage caches.
slides.narration: And then you run one word. Build. Behind that one word, five things happen in order. Your slides become a deck. Your narration goes to the voice engine and comes back as audio. A browser opens the deck and photographs every slide at full size. Those pictures and that audio become a video file. And your landing block becomes a finished page with the video already sitting in it. Every stage remembers what it already did. Change one line and it redoes that one line's worth of work.

slides.narration: Put the two next to each other. On the left, how I made my first one. Hand write the deck. Write a build script for that deck and no other. Record the narration in one sitting, and if you fluff a sentence near the end, do the whole pass again. And when you want a second webinar, start from nothing. On the right, how this one was made. Slides are a list. One command. The narration is written, so fixing a sentence is typing, not performing. And webinar number two starts by copying the file.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]Internal[/ACCENT] One
slides.sub: This is the objection people do not say out loud.
slides.narration: So that is the vehicle handled. Secret number two is a completely different kind of objection, and it is the one people almost never say to me directly. They tell me they are busy. They tell me they will get to it next quarter. But underneath, it is this one, and if you have ever felt it yourself you already know exactly what I am about to put on the screen.

slides.lie: "I would have to be on camera, and I hate my voice on video."
slides.truth: The truth: a [ACCENT]30-second sample[/ACCENT] records once and narrates forever.
slides.sub: You are never on camera. And you never do a second take.
slides.narration: I would have to be on camera, and I hate my voice on video. That is the one. And here is why it is wrong on both halves. You are never on camera at all, because the slides are the picture. The whole format is the picture. And as for your voice, you record about thirty seconds of clean speech, one time. The engine clones it locally, on your own machine, and from that point on it reads anything you type in that voice. You are not performing. You are typing. There is no take two, because there was never a take one.

slides.headline: Cloned [ACCENT]on your machine[/ACCENT], not in somebody's cloud
bullets: Ten to thirty seconds of clean speech is the entire sample
The model runs locally — your voice never leaves your server
Delivery is tuned steady for a long deck, not theatrical
Every slide is synthesized separately, so every slide is editable separately
No key, no per-character billing, no usage cap
slides.narration: Let me be specific about that, because voice cloning is a phrase you are right to be careful about. The sample is ten to thirty seconds of clean speech. The model runs on your own hardware, which means your voice is never uploaded anywhere, and the sample is deliberately kept out of anything you hand to somebody else. The delivery is tuned steady rather than dramatic on purpose, because across thirty nine slides, theatrical becomes exhausting. And there is no key, no per character bill and no cap, because there is nothing on the other end to do the billing.

slides.headline: What it costs to [ACCENT]fix a sentence[/ACCENT]
slides.narration: And this is the part I did not expect to matter nearly as much as it does. When you spot a clumsy sentence on slide twenty two, you change that sentence, and you run build again. One slide gets re synthesized. The other thirty eight are already done, so they are skipped entirely. Nothing gets re recorded, because nothing was ever recorded. And that single fact is the whole difference between a webinar you keep improving until it is genuinely good, and a webinar you ship once and never touch again because fixing it hurts too much.

slides.headline: You are not [ACCENT]performing[/ACCENT]. You are writing.
slides.sub: And writing is the part you have already been doing your whole life.
slides.narration: So take the entire camera problem and set it down, because it is not yours to carry. You are not performing anything. You are writing, and then a machine reads it back to people. If you can write an email explaining why somebody should buy the thing you sell, you can write this webinar, because that is all the narration field ever is. That is secret number two. Which brings us neatly to the one that actually costs people money.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]External[/ACCENT] One
slides.sub: This is the objection that is completely reasonable.
slides.narration: Secret number three, and I want to say something up front about this one. It is not a silly objection. It is completely reasonable, and the people who hold it are usually the ones who have already been burned once. If you have ever built something inside somebody else's platform and then watched the price move, or the terms change, or the export button quietly disappear underneath you, then this is the objection you are already thinking.

slides.lie: "Every tool that does this bills me monthly and owns my work."
slides.truth: The truth: it runs on [ACCENT]hardware you already pay for[/ACCENT], and you [ACCENT]keep it[/ACCENT].
slides.sub: It is a zip file. It runs on your server. There is nothing to cancel.
slides.narration: Every tool that does this bills me monthly and owns my work. That has been true, and that is precisely why this thing is built the way it is. What you get is a zip file. You put it on your own server and it runs there. The voice engine is on your machine. The renderer is on your machine. The page it produces is one self contained file that belongs to you. Nothing phones home, because there is nothing to phone. And there is no account to cancel, because there was never an account.

slides.headline: Four subscriptions to do what [ACCENT]one zip[/ACCENT] does
slides.narration: Let me put real numbers on the rented version of this. Webinar software runs around ninety nine dollars a month. Video hosting that does not stamp somebody else's branding across your player is about fifty nine. A page builder good enough to actually sell with is about ninety seven. And a voice or text to speech service with cloning is another ninety nine. That is three hundred and fifty four dollars every single month. Four thousand two hundred and forty eight a year. Over three years, twelve thousand seven hundred and forty four dollars, and at the end of it you own none of it.

bullets: It does not process payments — buy buttons are plain links to your checkout

slides.narration: And before I open the box, I want to tell you what is not in it, because you are going to find out anyway and I would much rather you heard it from me now. It does not process payments. The buy buttons are plain links and you point them at your own checkout. It does not send email. When somebody opts in, their address lands in a file on your server and you export it into whatever you already send with. It does not handle HTTPS, so for a public domain you put nginx or Caddy in front of it. And the voice engine has no password, so you keep it on loopback. None of that is difficult. All of it is honest.

slides.headline: That is the argument. Here is [ACCENT]what is in the box.[/ACCENT]
slides.sub: Nine pieces. Each one priced against what you would otherwise rent.
slides.narration: So that is the whole argument, and it is three sentences long. Making a webinar is one file and one command. You are never on camera and you never do a second take. And it runs on hardware you already pay for. Now let me open the box and show you the nine things you actually get, one at a time. And next to each one I am going to put what you would pay somewhere else for that same job, so that the number at the end is not a number I invented.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]local voice cloning engine[/ACCENT]

slides.narration: Number one. The voice engine. This is the piece that clones your voice from a short sample and then narrates anything you write in it, running entirely on your own hardware. It finds your graphics card if you have one and falls back to the processor if you do not. A cloud text to speech service with voice cloning runs about ninety nine dollars a month, so call this one eleven hundred and eighty eight dollars a year. slides.headline: The [ACCENT]presentation builder[/ACCENT] — nine layouts
slides.narration: Number two. The presentation builder. Nine layouts. Title, bullets, stats, compare, quote, myth, pricing, questions and call to action. Between them they cover every slide in this deck, and every slide in the thirty seven slide one that ships alongside it. You never touch markup once. Deck software runs about forty nine a month, so five hundred and eighty eight a year. Running total, seventeen hundred and seventy six.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]video renderer[/ACCENT]

stats.label: per year — render and hosting fees

slides.narration: Number three. The video renderer. It opens your deck in a browser, photographs every slide at full resolution, lines each picture up against its own piece of audio, and stitches the lot into one video file with clean fades between the slides. It renders slides in parallel, and you can turn that down if you are on a small server. Render and hosting fees run about fifty nine a month, so seven hundred and eight a year. Running total, twenty four hundred and eighty four.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]landing page builder[/ACCENT] — nine section types
slides.narration: Number four. The landing page builder. Nine section types. Hero, proof, problem, features, stack, pricing, testimonials, questions and close. You list the ones you want in the order you want them, and it writes one self contained page with the video already embedded in it. Styles inline, no external requests, nothing loading off somebody else's network. A page builder good enough to sell with is around ninety seven a month, so eleven hundred and sixty four a year. Running total, thirty six hundred and forty eight.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]built-in host[/ACCENT] with email capture

stats.label: per year — landing host with opt-ins

slides.narration: Number five. The host. One command serves the page and streams the video with seeking, so people can scrub through it instead of sitting there waiting. It catches opt ins from the gate on the page and appends them to a file you can read any time you like. It is written against the standard library only, so there is nothing extra to install and nothing to keep updated. A hosted landing page with opt in capture runs about thirty nine a month, so four hundred and sixty eight a year. Running total, forty one hundred and sixteen.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]legacy deck importer[/ACCENT]

stats.label: one-time — a manual conversion you skip

slides.narration: Number six. The importer, and this one exists purely because of my own mess. If you already have hand built webinar pages sitting in a folder somewhere, you point the importer at one along with your narration file, and it converts the whole deck into a config. It carries your narration across word for word, it maps the headings and the bullet slides and the myth beats, and then it tells you exactly which slides it could not classify so you know where to look. Call it two hundred and ninety seven. Running total, forty four hundred and thirteen.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]Docker setup[/ACCENT]

stats.label: one-time — an afternoon of setup you skip

slides.narration: Number seven. The Docker setup. A Dockerfile and a compose file, so that if you would rather not install ffmpeg and a browser and a Python environment directly on your host, you simply do not have to. The compose file publishes the voice engine on loopback only, which is the safe default, and I would leave it exactly that way. Call that an afternoon of your life you do not spend, so a hundred and ninety seven. Running total, forty six hundred and ten.

slides.headline: The [ACCENT]37-slide reference deck[/ACCENT]

stats.label: one-time — a real deck to pace against

slides.narration: Number eight. And if you have never written one of these before, this may quietly be the most useful thing in the whole box. A real thirty seven slide webinar, complete, in config form. Not a toy example. Around twenty one hundred words of narration, roughly fourteen minutes spoken. So when you are sitting in front of an empty file wondering how long a hook is meant to run, or where exactly the secrets go, you open that one and you copy the shape. Call it four hundred and ninety seven. Running total, fifty one hundred and seven.

You do not sit down and read the manual. You ask, and the thing answering you has already read it. Call that two hundred and ninety seven. Running total, five thousand four hundred and four.

sections.headline: Including the parts that are [ACCENT]not good news[/ACCENT]

items.q: Do I need a graphics card?
items.a: No. The engine auto-detects CUDA or Apple silicon and falls back to your CPU. CPU works — it is just slower, so start with a short deck before committing to a 40-slide one.

items.q: Does my voice sample leave my machine?
items.a: No. The model runs locally and nothing is uploaded. Samples are also excluded when you repackage the zip, because a sample is all anyone needs to generate unlimited speech in that person's voice.
No. Pricing buttons are plain links. You point them at your own Stripe, PayPal or checkout URL.
No. Opt-ins from the gate append to a JSONL file on your server. Export them into whatever you already send with.
No. The built-in server does not terminate TLS. For a public domain put nginx or Caddy in front of it, or copy the site folder to any static host.
It has no authentication. Anyone who can reach its port can synthesize any installed voice, so it binds to loopback by default. Keep it there unless you put an authenticating proxy in front of it.

items.q: Can I use it for more than one webinar?
items.a: Yes. Copy the config and change the words. There is no per-render fee, no cap and no seat count.

items.q: What if I already built webinars by hand?
items.a: The importer converts them. Narration carries across verbatim; headings, bullets, stats and myth beats are mapped where recognised, and anything it cannot classify is listed for you to review.

items.q: How long does a build take?
items.a: Voice synthesis dominates. For a 40-slide deck: roughly 5–15 minutes on a CUDA GPU, 15–40 on Apple silicon, hours on CPU alone. Video render is 3–15 minutes depending on hardware.
